sources.fact: Most women lose less than 16 teaspoons (80ml) of blood during their period, average around 6 to 8 teaspoons; heavy menstrual bleeding is 80ml or more per period, or lasting longer than 7 days; signs include changing products every hour or two; see your GP if worried about bleeding or periods get heavier
The endometrium is the tissue that sheds when you have your period, when implantation doesn't happen; period fluid is made up of endometrial cells and blood
Menstrual fluid consists of blood, cells, debris from the endometrial lining, mucus and other fluids; median loss about 40 ml; more than 80 ml per cycle is menorrhagia

math.note: 6 teaspoons x 5 ml = 30 ml (nidirect average 6 to 8 tsp)
8 teaspoons x 5 ml = 40 ml, matches EBSCO median about 40 ml
nidirect and EBSCO: heavy = 80 ml or more
nidirect: periods lasting longer than 7 days count as heavy

post.instagram_caption:
A whole period is usually just 6 to 8 teaspoons of blood 🥄

It looks like more because period fluid isn't only blood. Each month the womb builds a new lining, and if there's no pregnancy it sheds, so the flow is blood plus that lining plus mucus. Doctors call a period heavy at about 80 ml (16 teaspoons) or more.

See a doctor if you need a new pad every hour or two, or your period lasts more than 7 days.

Sources: nidirect (NHS info for Northern Ireland), Cleveland Clinic, EBSCO Research Starters.
